geschichte.metaTitel: History of Tarot Cards: From Tarocchi to 1909 | Tarot Cup
geschichte.metaBeschreibung: The history of tarot begins with a card game in 15th-century northern and central Italy. How it became a tool for readings from 1781, up to the 1909 cards.
geschichte.titel: The history of tarot: from the tarocchi to the cards of 1909
kurzantwort: Tarot began as a card game: in the 1440s, decks of playing cards with additional picture cards appeared in northern and central Italy. They were called *trionfi* and later *tarocchi*. Only from 1781 on did authors in France interpret the images as secret knowledge from ancient Egypt, a theory without evidence that is now considered disproved. From there, the path leads through the occultists of the 19th century to the cards of 1909.

abschnitte.titel: Where and when did tarot originate?
absaetze: Ordinary playing cards were already known in Europe in the 14th century. A few decades later, in northern Italy, picture cards showing figures and allegories were added to the four suits. They were called *trionfi*, meaning triumphs, and gave the game its first name; the word *tarocchi* did not catch on until around 1500.

The first reliable records date from the 1440s. At the court of the Este family in Ferrara, the painter Iacobo Sagramoro was paid in 1442 to paint four decks of such cards. A little earlier still, in September 1440, the notary Giusto Giusti of Anghiari in Tuscany noted in his diary that he had given Sigismondo Malatesta a deck of triumph cards, which he had had specially made in Florence with Malatesta’s coat of arms.

Where exactly the game was invented is an open question among researchers. Some place its origin around 1430 at the princely courts of Milan and Ferrara, others consider Ferrara the more likely place, and the find from Florence shows that the cards were known there very early, too. The festive processions at the courts and Petrarch’s 14th-century poem cycle “I Trionfi” are thought to be possible inspirations.

abschnitte.titel: Which early tarot cards have survived?
absaetze: The oldest surviving cards were made in the 1440s for the court of Milan, for Duke Filippo Maria Visconti and his son-in-law Francesco Sforza. Together with somewhat later decks from the following decades, they are known collectively as the Visconti-Sforza cards. They are hand-painted and decorated with gold leaf. They are usually attributed to the workshop of the painter Bonifacio Bembo; for one of the decks, his older brother is now also considered a possible painter.

None of these decks has survived complete. The cards are scattered across several collections, including the Beinecke Library at Yale University, the Morgan Library in New York, the Accademia Carrara in Bergamo, and the Pinacoteca di Brera in Milan. The watermarks may allow the 67 cards at Yale to be dated to 1441 or 1442. This deck probably once had at least 89 cards, including Faith, Hope, and Charity, as well as Knights and Pages in female form. It is therefore clearly different from the later structure of 78 cards.

abschnitte.titel: How was tarot played as a card game?
absaetze: Tarocchi was a trick-taking game. A player who could not follow the suit led had to trump with one of the picture cards; this makes tarot one of the very earliest games with trumps. The Fool had a special role: in the older versions of the game, it could be played to any trick instead of following suit or trumping, but it never won a trick.

Around 1500 the game reached France, probably through the French occupation of Milan at that time. There, a card pattern became established that is known today as the Tarot de Marseille: 78 cards, made up of four suits of 14 cards each, 21 numbered trumps, and the Fool. The name is younger than the cards and probably comes from the fact that many card makers in Marseille produced them; but the pattern was also printed in Paris, Avignon, and Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: When did people start using tarot for readings?
absaetze: Reading cards was already known in the 18th century, but people used ordinary playing cards for it. The practice took hold around 1760; people turned to tarot only about twenty years later.

The impetus came from Antoine Court de Gébelin, a Protestant pastor, scholar, and Freemason. In the eighth volume of his work “Le Monde primitif,” published in Paris in 1781, he declared the images of the trumps to be remnants of an ancient Egyptian book, which he called the “Book of Thoth.” The idea rested on the enthusiasm for Egypt in his day, not on evidence; scholars consider it disproved.

Two years later, Jean-Baptiste Alliette took up the idea. Under the name Etteilla, his surname spelled backward, he published some ten works on reading tarot between 1783 and 1786. In 1788 he had his own “corrected” deck engraved, meant to restore the images that card makers had supposedly corrupted. Tarot as a tool for readings begins with him.

abschnitte.titel: How did tarot become an esoteric teaching?
absaetze: In the 19th century, occultists in France developed the idea further. In 1856, Éliphas Lévi, born Alphonse-Louis Constant, linked tarot with Kabbalah and other teachings in his book on high magic. Paul Christian is credited with bringing the word “arcana,” meaning secrets, into use for the cards; it lives on to this day in the names [Major and Minor Arcana](/en/tarot/major-and-minor-arcana/).

Papus, whose real name was Gérard Encausse, published “Le Tarot des Bohémiens” in 1889. In the same year, Oswald Wirth drew 22 trumps modeled on the Tarot de Marseille; they appeared in Papus’s book and are considered the first attempt at an explicitly esoteric deck.

In England, these ideas were carried forward by the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, a secret society founded in London in 1888 by three Freemasons. In the order, tarot was part of the curriculum alongside Kabbalah, alchemy, and geomancy, among other subjects.

abschnitte.titel: What happened in 1909?
absaetze: The deck that still shapes how people picture tarot today also came from this circle. A former member of the Golden Dawn commissioned it in 1909 and wrote an accompanying book; the 78 cards were drawn by the artist [Pamela Colman Smith](/en/tarot/pamela-colman-smith/), whom he had met in the order. The deck was published in 1909 by Rider in London, although some sources give 1910 for the first printing. In the same year, Papus’s book “Le Tarot divinatoire” appeared in Paris, with 78 newly drawn cards by Jean-Gabriel Goulinat.

What set the deck apart was that the number cards of the [four suits](/en/tarot/tarot-suits/) show small scenes, too, instead of simply lining up wands, cups, swords, or pentacles. This made the images more accessible, and many later decks have taken up its motifs.
To find out how to read with these cards today, see [Tarot reading](/en/tarot/#ritual-schritt-fuer-schritt).

fragen.frage: Does tarot come from Egypt?
antwort: No. The idea comes from Antoine Court de Gébelin, who put it forward in 1781 without evidence. All early records point to 15th-century northern and central Italy, to Milan, Ferrara, and Florence; historians consider the Egypt theory disproved.

fragen.frage: How old are the oldest surviving tarot cards?
antwort: The oldest surviving cards were made in the 1440s for the court of Milan; some of them are now at Yale. Somewhat later cards from the same group are in New York, Bergamo, and Milan.

fragen.frage: Is tarot still played as a card game today?
antwort: Yes. In many European countries, such as France, Italy, Austria, and Hungary, tarot card games with their own rules are still played today.

fragen.frage: How long have tarot cards been used for readings?
antwort: Tarot readings are firmly documented mainly from the 1780s on, in France. Before that, for about 300 years, tarot was used mostly for playing, and people who read cards usually used ordinary playing cards.

arkana.metaTitel: Major and Minor Arcana: The 78 Cards Explained | Tarot Cup
arkana.metaBeschreibung: Tarot has 78 cards: 22 Major Arcana and 56 Minor Arcana. Where the names come from, how the trumps are numbered, and how you can tell the two groups apart.
arkana.titel: Major and Minor Arcana: how a tarot deck is structured
kurzantwort: Tarot consists of 78 cards in two groups: the 22 Major Arcana, that is, the trumps and the Fool, each with its own picture and name, and the 56 Minor Arcana, which are divided among four suits, each with ten number cards and four court cards. The names Major and Minor Arcana did not appear until the 19th century, in occult circles; before that, people simply spoke of trumps and suit cards. The order of the trumps is not the same in every deck, either.

abschnitte.titel: How is a tarot deck structured?
absaetze: A complete tarot deck has 78 cards. Of these, 56 are divided among four suits, much like ordinary playing cards. Each suit has ten number cards from the Ace to the Ten and four court cards, each showing a single figure. In addition, there are 21 numbered trumps and the Fool, a special card that stands outside the sequence. Together, the trumps and the Fool make up the 22 Major Arcana, and the 56 suit cards make up the Minor Arcana.
How the four suits came about and which figures belong to them is explained on the page [The four tarot suits](/en/tarot/tarot-suits/).

Not every deck stayed at 78 cards. In Italy, some tarocchi games are still played today with a different number of cards: the Tarocco Bolognese has 62 cards, the Tarocco Siciliano 64. The Florentine Minchiate, which died out in the early 20th century, even had 97. The Tarot de Marseille, which was printed in large numbers mainly in 18th-century France and Switzerland, also had 78 cards. The [history of tarot](/en/tarot/history/) tells how this came about.

abschnitte.titel: Where do the names Major and Minor Arcana come from?
absaetze: In 15th-century Italy, the additional cards with allegories were called *trionfi*, triumphs. In the language of card players, they are still simply the trumps today.

Arcana is the plural of arcanum, a word of Latin origin for a secret. It was applied to tarot by the French occultist Paul Christian, who brought terms such as “lames” and “arcanes” into use for the cards. Who first distinguished between Major and Minor Arcana is not settled; Paul Christian, Éliphas Lévi, and later authors from the same circle are named. According to most accounts, the names arose among French occultists in the second half of the 19th century, when tarot was already seen there as a tool for readings. Since then, the trumps have been called the Major Arcana and the suit cards the Minor Arcana.

abschnitte.titel: How are the Major Arcana numbered?
absaetze: In the Tarot de Marseille, the trumps usually bear Roman numerals and French names. The sequence begins with the Juggler as I and ends with the World as XXI. In between are, for example, the Popess as II, Justice as VIII, Strength as XI, and Judgement as XX. The numerals are often written additively, the Emperor, for instance, as IIII instead of IV. In this deck, the Fool has no number.

The sequence was never entirely uniform. In his 1980 book “The Game of Tarot,” Michael Dummett described three old Italian traditions: one around Florence and Bologna, one around Ferrara, and one around Milan. They differ in the order of the highest trumps and in whether the three virtues Justice, Strength, and Temperance are placed together. The Tarot de Marseille goes back to the Milanese sequence; in it, the three virtues stand apart, at positions VIII, XI, and XIV.

Practice varies widely when it comes to the Fool. In decks made for readings, it is often numbered 0, and sometimes it has no number at all; the Italian Tarocco Piemontese playing deck also numbers it 0. In the Central European tarock games, by contrast, it counts as the highest trump, in effect as 22.

abschnitte.titel: Why do Strength and Justice have different numbers?
absaetze: If you lay two decks side by side, you quickly notice a difference. In the Tarot de Marseille, Justice is VIII and Strength is XI. On the cards of 1909 with the pictures by Pamela Colman Smith, it is the other way around: there, Strength is VIII and Justice is XI.

The swap is one of a series of changes made by occult circles in England. Because tarot cards were hardly known there, they were able to redesign pictures and symbols quite freely. Names changed, too: the Juggler became the Magician, the Pope became the Hierophant, and the Popess became the High Priestess. So the new numbering comes from this milieu and not from the tradition of the old playing cards.

Because many later decks follow the pictures of 1909, you come across both numberings today; neither of them is wrong. You can find more about the artist behind these pictures on the page about [Pamela Colman Smith](/en/tarot/pamela-colman-smith/).

abschnitte.titel: How can you tell Major and Minor Arcana apart in a spread?
absaetze: The quickest way to tell the groups apart is by the picture. A Major Arcana card bears a number and a name of its own, such as VII and “The Chariot.” A number card, by contrast, shows the symbol of its suit in the matching quantity. On the cards of 1909, the number cards also bear a Roman numeral, but on the Four of Pentacles you still see four pentacles, even though they are worked into a small scene. Court cards show a single figure with the symbol of their suit.

In the tradition, the two groups carry different weight. The Major Arcana are seen as pointing to larger themes and turning points, the Minor Arcana more to what happens in everyday life. You can find a short overview of both groups under [What is tarot?](/en/tarot/#was-ist-tarot).

The occult authors focused mainly on the trumps. Antoine Court de Gébelin discussed the 22 trumps at length in 1781, and in 1889 Oswald Wirth drew only these 22 cards. Etteilla, on the other hand, read with all 78 cards and had his own deck engraved for this at the end of the 1780s. For a long time, the number cards mostly showed only their suit symbols. There were early exceptions such as the Sola Busca tarot of 1491, but scenes on the number cards became widely known mainly through the cards of 1909.

fragen.frage: How many Major and Minor Arcana are there?
antwort: A complete tarot deck has 22 Major Arcana and 56 Minor Arcana, 78 cards in all. The Minor Arcana are divided into four suits of 14 cards each.

fragen.frage: Is the Fool card 0 or 22?
antwort: That depends on the deck and on how it is used. In the Tarot de Marseille, the Fool has no number; in decks made for readings, it is often numbered 0; and in Central European tarock games, it counts as the highest trump.

fragen.frage: What number is the Strength card?
antwort: In the Tarot de Marseille, it is XI; on the cards of 1909 and many decks after them, it is VIII. In each case, Justice has the other of the two numbers.

fragen.frage: Can you read tarot with just the Major Arcana?
antwort: Yes. Court de Gébelin and many occult authors of the 19th century were mainly concerned with the 22 trumps. With all 78 cards, though, a spread speaks with more voices, because everyday life is part of it, too.

farben.metaTitel: Tarot Suits: Wands, Cups, Swords, Pentacles | Tarot Cup
farben.metaBeschreibung: The four tarot suits go back to Italian playing cards. Where Wands, Cups, Swords, and Pentacles come from and how their meanings developed.
farben.titel: The four tarot suits: Wands, Cups, Swords, and Pentacles
kurzantwort: Tarot has four suits: Wands, Cups, Swords, and Pentacles. They come from the Italian playing cards of the late Middle Ages, where they are called *bastoni*, *coppe*, *spade*, and *denari*, so they are older than any way of reading the cards. The link to areas of life and to the elements that is common today goes back only to occult authors of the 19th and early 20th centuries.

abschnitte.titel: Where do the four suits come from?
absaetze: Playing cards appear in Europe toward the end of the 14th century. The first mentions date from the 1370s, for example from Florence, Paris, and Viterbo. The cards probably reached Italy and Spain from the Islamic world. A surviving deck from the Mamluk Sultanate, now in the Topkapı Palace in Istanbul, was not made until the 15th or early 16th century, but it shows the same four suits: coins, cups, swords, and batons. It is seen as an indication of what the models for the European cards may have looked like.

In Italy, these suits are still called *bastoni*, *coppe*, *spade*, and *denari* today, meaning batons, cups, swords, and coins. Together with the very similar Spanish cards, they are known as the Latin suits. The batons may originally have been polo sticks. On Italian-style cards, such as those common in northeastern Italy, the batons are straight and cross each other on the number cards to form a lattice; the mostly curved swords cross, too. On Spanish-style cards, the batons are knobbly clubs, and both batons and swords stand separately side by side.

When the trumps were added in northern and central Italy in the 15th century, the new game kept these four suits. Even the oldest surviving tarot cards, painted for the court of Milan, show cups, swords, batons, and coins.

abschnitte.titel: Why are Pentacles sometimes called Coins?
absaetze: The names of the suits have shifted over time. On the cards of 1909, the batons became Wands and the coins became Pentacles. Other decks speak of Discs. The other suits have alternative names, too, such as Scepters or Rods instead of Wands, and Grails or Goblets instead of Cups.

Whatever the name, it is always the same suit. If you read with a different deck than the one in the app, you will quickly find your way once you know that Coins, Pentacles, and Discs belong together.
Incidentally, there are also tarot decks for card games with the French suits of hearts, diamonds, clubs, and spades. For readings, the Italian symbols have remained the norm.

abschnitte.titel: Which court cards belong to each suit?
absaetze: In tarot, each suit has 14 cards: ten number cards from the Ace to the Ten and four court cards. On the cards of 1909, these are Page, Knight, Queen, and King; in the Tarot de Marseille, King, Queen, Knight, and Page.

This gives tarot one figure more than most ordinary card games. Italian decks with Latin suits today usually have King, Knight, and Page, but no Queen. The French deck has King, Queen, and Jack, but no Knight. In tarot, the Knight and the Queen stand side by side.

Before 1909, the number cards usually looked plain and showed their suit symbol as many times as their number. On the cards of 1909, each number card was given a little scene of its own; you can read more on the page about [Pamela Colman Smith](/en/tarot/pamela-colman-smith/).

abschnitte.titel: What do the four suits stand for in the tradition?
absaetze: In today’s tradition, each suit has its own domain and its own element. Wands belong to action and fire, Cups to feelings and water, Swords to thoughts and air, and Pentacles to the tangible and earth. You can find a short overview under [What is tarot?](/en/tarot/#was-ist-tarot).

This scheme is considerably younger than the cards. When the suits arrived in Italy, they were the symbols of a game. Only when occultists in the 19th century linked tarot with Kabbalah, numerology, and other teachings did the four suits also gain a fixed place in a larger system of thought. This very scheme appears, for example, in the work of the Russian esotericist Pyotr Ouspensky (also spelled Uspensky), whose book on the symbolism of tarot was written in 1911 and published in 1913. He equated Wands, Cups, Swords, and Pentacles with fire, water, air, and earth, and at the same time with the four letters of the Hebrew name of God.

To this day, the assignment is not uniform; some authors, for example, assign air to Wands and fire to Swords. There is also an old conjecture about where the symbols came from: they may once have stood for the estates of society, with swords for the nobility, cups for the clergy, coins for the merchants, and batons for the peasants. As early as 1781, Court de Gébelin linked the four suits with the estates of society as part of his Egypt theory. There is no evidence for this; the Victoria and Albert Museum mentions it only as a possibility.

abschnitte.titel: How do you read the suits in a spread?
absaetze: Many people who read tarot first look at which suits have come up once the cards are revealed. If several Cups lie together, the tradition reads this as a sign that feelings are playing a bigger role at the moment; many Swords turn the focus more toward thoughts and decisions. If a suit is missing altogether, that, too, can be worth asking about.

The Major Arcana belong to no suit. The page [Major and Minor Arcana](/en/tarot/major-and-minor-arcana/) explains how to tell them apart from the suit cards. In many approaches, whether a card is upright or reversed adds a second layer; you can read more under [Reversed tarot cards](/en/tarot/reversed-tarot-cards/).

fragen.frage: Are Pentacles and Coins the same suit?
antwort: Yes. In Italy, the suit is called *denari*, meaning coins; on the cards of 1909, it is called Pentacles, and in other decks Discs. It is always the same one of the four suits.

fragen.frage: Why doesn’t tarot have hearts, diamonds, clubs, and spades?
antwort: Because it originated in Italy, where people played with batons, cups, swords, and coins. For card games, however, there are also tarot decks with French suits.

fragen.frage: Which element goes with which tarot suit?
antwort: In the scheme most common today, Wands go with fire, Cups with water, Swords with air, and Pentacles with earth. This scheme comes from occult authors and is not the same everywhere.

fragen.frage: How many cards are in each tarot suit?
antwort: Each suit has 14 cards: ten number cards from the Ace to the Ten and four court cards. Together, the four suits make up the 56 Minor Arcana.

umgekehrt.metaTitel: Reversed Tarot Cards: What They Can Mean | Tarot Cup
umgekehrt.metaBeschreibung: Reversed tarot cards have a long history: how long people have read them, the ways of reading them, and how reversals come about when you shuffle.
umgekehrt.titel: Reversed tarot cards: origins, readings, and shuffling
kurzantwort: A reversed tarot card lies upside down when you reveal it: from where you sit, the picture is the wrong way up. The book of 1770 that is considered the oldest manual of card reading already gives cards a meaning of their own for this position; by 1791 at the latest, this also applied to tarot cards, and in the 19th century, reversals were a firm part of tarot. Whether you read reversals, and how, is still a matter of tradition and your own choice.

abschnitte.titel: What does “reversed” mean in tarot?
absaetze: Every tarot card has a top and a bottom. If you see the figure the right way up after revealing the card, it is upright. If the picture is upside down, the card is called reversed. What counts is always the view of the person reading the cards.

The guide sums up briefly under [Upright and reversed](/en/tarot/#aufrecht-und-umgekehrt) what a reversed card usually means in readings today. This page is about everything around it: where the custom comes from, the different ways of handling it, and how reversed cards come about in the first place when you shuffle.

abschnitte.titel: When did people start reading reversed cards?
absaetze: The trail leads to Paris. In 1770, a slim book appeared there that is considered the oldest manual of card reading in the West. Its author was Jean-Baptiste Alliette, who called himself Etteilla, his surname spelled backward. At that time, he did not yet read with tarot, but with the 32 cards of a piquet deck and one additional card that was blank on both sides.

Even in this book, a card has two meanings, one for the upright position and one for the reversed position. Etteilla marks the second with an R and describes it as a card turned from top to bottom. For him, the King of Diamonds, for example, stands for one man when upright and for another man when reversed; the Jack of Diamonds stands for a soldier when upright and for a servant when reversed.

From 1783 on, Etteilla also wrote about tarot. From 1791 on, a deck of 33 cards was also published under his name, with explanations on the cards that can be read in either direction. The page [History of tarot](/en/tarot/history/) tells how tarot became a tool for readings in the first place.

abschnitte.titel: How did reversals become part of tarot?
absaetze: In tarot, reversals are documented by 1791 at the latest. That year saw the publication of a dictionary of Etteilla’s tarot, which he called the “Book of Thoth”; it was written by a member of the society Etteilla had founded to interpret these cards. Right at the beginning, it says that every card allows two interpretations, one upright and one reversed. A hundred years later, this was common practice in the manuals.

In 1889, the French occultist Papus wrote that anyone following the usual manuals had to memorize the meanings of all 78 cards upright and again reversed, plus rules for when certain cards appear together, about 200 meanings in all. He wanted to spare his readers most of this rote learning and proposed a simpler system with a few basic concepts.

The playing card historian Thierry Depaulis describes card reading in general this way: in a reading, the position of a card, upright or reversed, counts just as much as the order in which it appears. At the same time, he notes that the meanings given to figures and suits are a matter of choice. So there is no generally valid rule for reversals, but rather different traditions.

A more recent book shows how varied the approaches have become: in 2002, the tarot author Mary K. Greer devoted more than 250 pages to reversed cards and presented twelve different approaches to reading them.

abschnitte.titel: How can you read a reversed card?
absaetze: If you read with reversals today, you can choose among several approaches. Often, a reversed card is read as the same theme in a toned-down form: what sounds strong when upright is quieter or still taking shape when reversed.

Others see it as something blocked or delayed, a force that cannot flow unhindered at the moment. A third approach turns the card inward. It then speaks less of what is happening around you than of what is going on inside you. The older handbooks, by contrast, often gave reversed cards a meaning entirely of their own, as Etteilla did with his Jack of Diamonds.

And some people read without any reversals at all, reading every card as upright even when it falls the other way up. None of these approaches is more correct than another. What helps is simply to decide on one approach before you shuffle and to stick with it throughout a spread.

abschnitte.titel: How do reversed cards come about when you shuffle?
absaetze: A new deck usually lies in its box with all the pictures facing the same way. If you shuffle in a way that keeps the cards facing the same way, you get hardly any reversals. If you want some, you can help things along a little as you shuffle.

One simple way: split the deck into two halves, turn one of them so that top and bottom swap, and slide the two halves back into each other. Others spread the cards face down on the table, swirl them around with both hands, and then push them back into a pile. And if you don’t straighten out cards that fell reversed after a spread, their reversals stay in the deck. Incidentally, Etteilla already advised shuffling thoroughly and without looking in 1770.

Pay attention to how you reveal the cards, too. If you turn a card over its top edge, it ends up upside down. So always turn the cards over the same way, preferably sideways, as the guide describes under [Tarot reading step by step](/en/tarot/#ritual-schritt-fuer-schritt).

fragen.frage: Is a reversed tarot card a bad sign?
antwort: No. In many readings today, it speaks of the same theme as when upright, just with a different emphasis. You can read more under [Upright and reversed](/en/tarot/#aufrecht-und-umgekehrt).

fragen.frage: Do I have to read reversed cards?
antwort: No. Reading with reversals and reading without them are both part of the tradition, and even experienced readers often leave them out. All that matters is that you stick with your decision throughout a spread.

fragen.frage: Were reversals used with the earliest tarot cards?
antwort: There is no evidence for that. In 15th-century Italy, tarot was used for playing; readings with tarot cards are documented only from the late 18th century.

fragen.frage: How often does a card come up reversed?
antwort: That depends on how you shuffle. If half of the deck has been turned and everything is shuffled well, roughly every other card lies upside down. Without turning, reversals come up only rarely.

app.titel: Draw a card and see how it falls
text: In Tarot Cup, every card can fall upright or reversed, both about equally often. You can find the available spreads under [Tarot reading](/en/tarot/#legungen).

smith.metaTitel: Pamela Colman Smith and the 1909 Tarot Art | Tarot Cup
smith.metaBeschreibung: Pamela Colman Smith drew all 78 cards of the best-known tarot deck in 1909. Her life led from London via Jamaica and New York to Cornwall.
smith.titel: Pamela Colman Smith and the tarot images of 1909
kurzantwort: Pamela Colman Smith (1878–1951) was an artist from London who in 1909 drew all 78 images of a tarot deck that is still among the most widely used today. Before that, she worked for the theater, illustrated books, and exhibited in New York at Alfred Stieglitz’s gallery. Her cards made scenes on the number cards widely known, but her own name long remained in the background.

abschnitte.titel: Where did Pamela Colman Smith come from?
absaetze: Pamela Colman Smith was born in London in 1878 to American parents. When she was about ten years old, her father’s work took the family to Kingston, Jamaica, for a time. She later passed on the tales of West Indian tradition that she came to know there in books of her own, such as “Annancy Stories” in 1899.
In 1893, she began studying at the Pratt Institute in Brooklyn, which had only been founded a few years earlier. Her teacher was Arthur Wesley Dow. In 1897, she left the school without a degree.

abschnitte.titel: What did she do in the theater?
absaetze: As early as the 1890s, she was close to the actress Ellen Terry and Terry’s daughter Edith Craig, and so belonged to the circle around the Lyceum Theatre, where Henry Irving also worked. In 1899, she moved back to London. Bram Stoker, business manager of the Lyceum and author of “Dracula,” had her draw the program for an American tour. She traveled with the company for seven months, sketching along the way and even taking small parts on stage herself. She also designed costumes and sets for this circle.
Ellen Terry called her “Pixie,” and she soon became known by that nickname. From 1903 on, Smith published a small magazine of her own, “The Green Sheaf,” which ran to thirteen issues.

abschnitte.titel: How did she find her way to the Golden Dawn and to Stieglitz?
absaetze: In 1901, she joined the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, an occult secret society. She had been introduced by the poet William Butler Yeats.

Alfred Stieglitz showed her drawings in his gallery in New York, the Little Galleries of the Photo-Secession. She was the first artist to exhibit there whose work was not photography. A contemporary reported that the exhibition was extended and that about half of the main collection on display found buyers. In 1907, Stieglitz also photographed some of her drawings himself; the Philadelphia Museum of Art now holds such photographs.
Three works on paper now in the Tate in London also date from 1907. They are named after pieces of music by Grieg, Sinding, and Mozart.

abschnitte.titel: How did the 1909 cards come about?
absaetze: In the Golden Dawn, Smith also met the man who commissioned a new tarot deck in 1909. Like her, he had been a member of the order; in 1903, Smith had joined the branch of the order that he led. You can read more about the commission and the accompanying book on the page [History of tarot](/en/tarot/history/#the-cards-of-1909).

Smith was to draw all 78 images. For the Major Arcana, she received precise instructions, while for the Minor Arcana she could largely work as she saw fit. The deck was published in 1909 by Rider in London, although some sources give 1910 for the first printing. By her own account, she was paid far too little for so much work. The page [Major and Minor Arcana](/en/tarot/major-and-minor-arcana/) explains how the Major and Minor Arcana differ.

abschnitte.titel: What is special about her images?
absaetze: In older decks, the number cards of the four suits usually show only their symbols, such as seven cups or three swords, neatly arranged. Smith gave each of these cards a small scene of its own, with people, landscapes, and gestures. This means that the number cards, too, can be looked at like pictures. Smith did not invent this idea, but her cards made it widely known, and it has had a lasting influence on later decks. You can find out what defines the four suits under [The four tarot suits](/en/tarot/tarot-suits/).

There was a model as early as the 15th century: the Sola Busca tarot, probably engraved in Ferrara in 1491 and regarded as the oldest complete surviving deck of 78 cards, shows figures and scenes on its number cards. Photographs of it were on display at the British Museum in London in 1908. About a dozen cards show echoes of this model; opinions differ on how closely Smith followed it overall.

abschnitte.titel: What happened in her later life?
absaetze: From 1911, Smith lived in New York for several years, and during this time she joined the Catholic Church. After the First World War, she moved to Cornwall; in the early 1920s, an inheritance allowed her to buy a house on the Lizard Peninsula. With Nora Lake, with whom she lived, she later ran a house where Catholic priests could go on retreat.

Pamela Colman Smith died in Bude, Cornwall, in 1951, with no money and little reputation as an artist. Only in recent years has she returned to the spotlight: in 2019, the Pratt Institute devoted an exhibition to her, and from 2022 to 2023, the Whitney Museum in New York showed her work in an exhibition on early American modernism.

fragen.frage: Did Pamela Colman Smith draw all 78 tarot cards?
antwort: Yes, both the Major and the Minor Arcana. She received fixed instructions mainly for the Major Arcana; she largely designed the scenes on the number cards herself.

fragen.frage: Where do the card images in Tarot Cup come from?
antwort: The card images in Tarot Cup were drawn by Pamela Colman Smith. They were published in 1909 and are in the public domain. They are based on scans of the original print from Wikimedia Commons; you can find out more under [Image credits and licenses](/en/image-credits-and-licenses/).

fragen.frage: Was Pamela Colman Smith American?
antwort: Her parents were American, but she was born in London in 1878. She spent her youth between England, Jamaica, and New York, where she studied and later exhibited.

fragen.frage: Where can you see her art today?
antwort: Her works are held by the Tate in London and the Whitney Museum in New York, among others; the Whitney has, for example, the drawing “The Wave” from 1903. Her tarot images are known above all from the many editions of the deck.

app.titel: Draw the 1909 images in the app
text: In Tarot Cup, you draw cards with Pamela Colman Smith’s images, taken from the original print and only cropped to the picture area. You can find the available spreads under [Tarot reading](/en/tarot/#legungen).
